'''''Celtis australis''''', the '''European nettle tree''', '''European hackberry''', '''Mediterranean hackberry''', '''lote tree''', '''southern nettle tree''', or honey<!--DOES NOT redirect here, boldface not correct-->berry,<ref name=EPPO>{{cite web |title=''Celtis australis'' |url=https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/CETAU |publisher=[[European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization]] (EPPO) |access-date=27 May 2025}}</ref><ref>Bailey, L.H.; Bailey, E.Z.; the staff of the Liberty Hyde Bailey Hortorium. 1976. ''Hortus third: A concise dictionary of plants cultivated in the United States and Canada''. Macmillan, New York.</ref> is a [[deciduous]] tree native to Southern Europe, North Africa, and [[Asia Minor]].

==Description==
The tree can grow to {{Convert|25|m}} in height, though {{Convert|10|m|abbr=on}} is more common in cooler climates. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is smooth and grey, almost elephantine.<ref name=More>More, D. & White, J. (2003).''Trees of Britain & Northern Europe'', p. 417. Cassells, London. {{ISBN|0-304-36192-5}}.</ref>

The alternate [[leaves]] are narrow and sharp-toothed, rugose above and tomentose below, {{Convert|5–15|cm|frac=4}} long and dark grey/green throughout the year, fading to a pale yellow before falling in autumn.

The apetalous wind-pollinated flowers are [[perfect flower|perfect]] (hermaphrodite, having both male and female organs), small and green, either singly or in small clusters.

The fruit is a small, dark-purple berry-like [[drupe]], 1 cm wide, hanging in short clusters. 

== Distribution and habitat ==
The plant prefers light well-drained (sandy) and medium (loamy) soils, including those nutritionally poor; it can tolerate drought but not shade. The [[Mediterranean climate]] is especially suitable for the plant but it can tolerate colder climate (USDA Zone 7B). An article on Nettle tree cultivation is brought down in [[Ibn al-'Awwam]]'s 12th-century agricultural work, ''Book on Agriculture''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Ibn al-'Awwam |first=Yahya |author-link=Ibn al-'Awwam |url=https://archive.org/details/lelivredelagric00algoog/page/n14/mode/2up |title=Le livre de l'agriculture d'Ibn-al-Awam (kitab-al-felahah) |publisher=Paris, A. Franck |year=1864 |location=Paris |pages=311–312 (ch. 7 - Article 38) |language=fr |translator=J.-J. Clement-Mullet |oclc=780050566}} (pp. [[iarchive:lelivredelagric00algoog/page/n418/mode/2up|311]]-312 (Article XXXVIII)</ref>

Archaeological evidence which supports the opinion that the tree is native to the Levant; ''Celtis australis'' seeds were discovered at an Iron Age dig in Tel Rehov, Israel. Wooden shards from the tree were also discovered there, as well as at Tel Jezreel, another site in Israel.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Early finds of Celtis australis in the southern Levant |url=https://cris.biu.ac.il/en/publications/early-finds-of-celtis-australis-in-the-southern-levant/}}</ref> The tree still grows wild in many places in the country, such as Mt. Carmel, the Galilee, the Golan Heights, Samaria, and the Judean Mountains,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Flora of Israel and adjacent areas |url=https://flora.org.il/en/plants/celaus/}}</ref> and is one of the many trees used for public landscaping in Tel Aviv.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tree Survey at Rabin Square, Tel Aviv Municipality |url=https://www.tel-aviv.gov.il/Forms/%D7%A1%D7%A7%D7%A8%20%D7%A2%D7%A6%D7%99%D7%9D%20%D7%AA%D7%97%D7%A0%D7%AA%20%D7%A8%D7%91%D7%99%D7%9F.pdf}}</ref>

The species likes to stand with a mix of other kinds of trees, in wooded ravines, by streams. It thrives anywhere from sea level to 1,200 metres.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ARBOLAPP Celtis australis European nettle tree |work=Arbolapp |url=https://www.arbolapp.es/en/species/info/celtis-australis/}}</ref>

The tree was introduced to England in 1796.<ref name="Hillier">Hillier Nurseries Ltd. (1977). ''Hilliers' Manual of Trees & Shrubs, 4th edition'', p.70. David & Charles, Newton Abbott, UK. {{ISBN|0-7153-7460-5}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
The drupes are extremely popular with birds and other wildlife. Its diminutive, green-tinted flowers also attract pollinators.<ref>{{Cite web |title=EUFORGEN Celtis australis European nettle tree |url=https://www.euforgen.org/species/celtis-australis}}</ref>

== Uses ==
Trade names for the species include nettle wood and brimji.<ref name="ref83merij">{{Cite web |title=Celtis australis (Ulmaceae): Nettle Wood, Brimji. |url=http://www.worldagroforestry.org/treedb/AFTPDFS/Celtis_australis.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130927114041/http://www.worldagroforestry.org/treedb/AFTPDFS/Celtis_australis.pdf |archive-date=2013-09-27 |access-date=2012-08-28}}</ref> It is often planted as an [[Ornamental plant|ornamental]] as it is long-living and resistant to air pollution.

The fruit is sweet and edible raw or cooked. The leaves and fruit are astringent, lenitive, and stomachic. A [[decoction]] of both the leaves and fruit is used in the treatment of [[amenorrhoea]], heavy menstrual and inter-menstrual bleeding, and colic. The decoction can also be used to astringe the mucous membranes in the treatment of [[diarrhea]], [[dysentery]], and peptic ulcers. A yellow dye is obtained from the bark.

The wood is very tough, pliable, durable, and widely used by turners; the flexible, thin shoots are used as walking sticks.

=== Secondary metabolites ===
The leaves of ''Celtis australis'' are a rich source of [[flavonoid]] {{Nowrap|C-glycosides}}.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Spitaler, R |author2=Gurschler, S |author3=Ellmerer, E |author4=Schubert, B |author5=Sgarbossa, M |author6=Zidorn, C |year=2009 |title=Flavonoids from Celtis australis (Cannabaceae) |journal=Biochemical Systematics and Ecology |volume=37 |issue=2 |pages=120–121 |bibcode=2009BioSE..37..120S |doi=10.1016/j.bse.2008.11.020 |issn=0305-1978}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author1=Kaltenhauser, M |author2=Ellmerer, EP |author3=Zidorn, C |year=2010 |title=Rhamnopyranosylvitexin derivatives from Celtis australis |journal=Journal of the Serbian Chemical Society |volume=75 |issue=6 |pages=733–738 |doi=10.2298/JSC090817049K |issn=1820-7421 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Young leaves of ''C. australis'' from Northern Italy were found to contain the highest amounts of phenolics per gram dry weight. Amounts rapidly decreased until mid-May and after this date the level of phenolics fluctuated but showed no discernible trend. This general trend of high amounts of phenolics in the early growing season and a fast decline affected both [[caffeic acid]] derivatives and [[flavonoid]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Sommavilla, V |author2=Haidacher-Gasser, D |author3=Sgarbossa, M |author4=Zidorn, C |year=2012 |title=Seasonal variation in phenolics in leaves of Celtis australis (Cannabaceae) |journal=Biochemical Systematics and Ecology |volume=41 |pages=110–114 |bibcode=2012BioSE..41..110S |doi=10.1016/j.bse.2011.12.028 |issn=0305-1978}}</ref>

== In culture ==
''Celtis australis'' is supposed to have been the Lotus of the ancients, whose fruit [[Herodotus]], [[Dioscorides]], and [[Theophrastus]] describe as sweet, pleasant, and wholesome. [[Homer]] has [[Odysseus|Ulysses]] refer to the "[[Lotus-eaters]]" and the "lotus" in ''Odyssey, Book IX''.<ref name="Keeler">{{cite book |last=Keeler |first=Harriet L. |url=https://archive.org/details/ournativetreesa02keelgoog |title=Our Native Trees and How to Identify Them |publisher=Charles Scribner's Sons |year=1900 |location=New York |pages=[https://archive.org/details/ournativetreesa02keelgoog/page/n278 249]–252}}</ref>[[File:Barjols2013 016.jpg|thumb|right|170px|In [[Fox-Amphoux]], France, planted 1550]]

In Islamic tradition, hackberry trees are considered holy and amulets made from their wood are employed to exorcise demons. The hackberry trees on the [[Temple Mount]] in [[Jerusalem]] are said to be the oldest in the world.<ref>[https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2022-01-20/ty-article-magazine/.premium/jerusalems-oldest-guardians-hackberry-trees-on-the-temple-mount/0000017f-ef84-d8a1-a5ff-ff8e59770000 Jerusalem's Oldest Guardians: Hackberry Trees on the Temple Mount], [[Haaretz]]</ref> 

A large specimen planted in 1550 stands before the church in the [[village perché]] of [[Fox-Amphoux]] in the [[Provence]] region of southern France. The tree was {{Convert|18|m|abbr=on}} in height with a [[diameter at breast height|circumference at breast height]] of 5 m in 2013.<ref>{{Cite web |date=24 April 2009 |title=Micocoulier, Fox-Amphoux (Var) |url=http://krapooarboricole.wordpress.com/2009/04/25/micocoulier-fox-amphoux-var/}}</ref>

The fruit and its effects are described in [[Alfred Tennyson]]'s poem ''[[The Lotos-Eaters]]''.
